pos: v. (to move toward, to arrive; rendering Hebrew bo, Greek erchomai)
etymology: Old English cuman, among the most ancient words in the language. In Scripture it is the great verb of invitation — and the Bible's last prayer.
biblical_def: To come is to move toward and arrive, and Scripture hangs the gospel on it. “Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden” (Mat 11:28); “him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out” (Joh 6:37). The direction is everything: not first a doing but a drawing near, empty-handed, to a Person. The Bible closes with the word running both ways — the Spirit and the bride say Come, and the church answers, Even so, come, Lord Jesus.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines come as to move toward, to advance nearer, in any manner and by any means — the plainest of motions, which grace makes the whole of faith's beginning.
webster_full: COME, v.i. To move toward; to advance nearer, in any manner and by any means.
2. To draw nigh; to approach; to arrive.
3. To advance and arrive at some state or condition; as, to come to pass.
scriptures: Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.
Joh 6:37
All that the Father giveth me shall come to me; and him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.
Isa 55:1
Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, and he that hath no money; come ye, buy, and eat; yea, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price.
And the Spirit and the bride say, Come. And let him that heareth say, Come. And let him that is athirst come. And whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely.
corruption_summary: The age has kept the word and reversed its object — come to the event, come to the experience, come as you are and stay as you came — while the Person to whom the call points is made optional.
corruption_paragraphs: Every gospel invitation in Scripture terminates on Christ Himself: come unto me. Modern religious marketing terminates on the venue — the service, the group, the atmosphere. A sinner can answer that call perfectly and never arrive anywhere, because a venue cannot give rest. The old call is grammatically ruthless: one verb, one object, and the object is a Person who receives all comers and casts out none.

The other corruption keeps the sinner's inability and deletes the command — since no man can come except the Father draw him (Joh 6:44), why call? But Scripture puts the impossibility and the invitation in the same chapter without embarrassment. The call itself is the cord by which the Father draws; whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely (Rev 22:17).
roots_summary: Hebrew bo (H935), to come or enter, one of the commonest verbs in the Old Testament; Greek erchomai (G2064), whose imperative is the gospel's open door and the church's final prayer.
roots_lines: Hebrew bo (H935) — to come, go in, enter; Noah into the ark, Israel into the land, the King into His city.
Greek erchomai (G2064) — to come; “Come and see” (Joh 1:39), “come unto me” (Mat 11:28), “Even so, come, Lord Jesus” (Rev 22:20).
usage: “Come unto me, all ye that labour” — the invitation terminates on Christ, not on an event.
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out” — the double negative of welcome.
“And the Spirit and the bride say, Come” — the last page keeps the first invitation open.

pos: v. (to move, proceed, depart; rendering Hebrew halak, Greek poreuomai)
etymology: Old English gan. If come is the gospel's first verb toward Christ, go is its first verb from Him — the church exists between the two.
biblical_def: To go is to set out. Scripture's discipleship begins with it — Abram is told “Get thee out” before he is told anything else — and the risen Christ's commission turns the whole church outward with it: “Go ye therefore, and teach all nations” (Mat 28:19); “Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature” (Mar 16:15). The verb of the Samaritan's mercy is the same: “Go, and do thou likewise” (Luk 10:37). Grace gathers in order to send.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines go as to move, to pass, to walk, to proceed — motion generally, without reference to manner; Scripture gives the motion its errand.
webster_full: GO, v.i. To move; to pass; to proceed from one place, state or station to another.
2. To walk; to move on the feet or step by step.
3. To depart; to move from a place, opposed to come.
scriptures: Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost:
And he said unto them, Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature.
Jos 1:9
Have not I commanded thee? Be strong and of a good courage; be not afraid, neither be thou dismayed: for the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest.
And he said, He that shewed mercy on him. Then said Jesus unto him, Go, and do thou likewise.
corruption_summary: The commission's go has been traded for an architectural come — missions outsourced to professionals, mercy outsourced to programs — while the disciple's own feet stay home.
corruption_paragraphs: The grammar of Matthew 28 puts the going on every disciple, and the promise beside it — “lo, I am with you alway” — is a traveling mercy, not a sanctuary fixture. A church that has reversed the verbs, expecting the world to come while the saints sit, has not lost its nerve so much as its grammar. Joshua's charge holds for the sent church: “be not afraid… for the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest” (Jos 1:9).

The opposite corruption is going without being sent — activity as identity, motion as righteousness. Scripture's go is always an errand with a Sender, a message, and a neighbour: teach all nations; preach the gospel; do thou likewise. Going that carries no gospel and binds up no wounds is travel, not obedience.
roots_summary: Hebrew halak (H1980), to walk or go — the root of the Old Testament's walking with God; Greek poreuomai (G4198), to proceed on a journey, the commission's own verb.
roots_lines: Hebrew halak (H1980) — to go, to walk; Enoch walked with God, and Micah 6:8 asks a man to walk humbly with Him.
Greek poreuomai (G4198) — to go, journey; Matthew 28:19, Luke 10:37, and the Lord's own going to prepare a place (Joh 14:2).
usage: “Go ye therefore, and teach all nations” — the church's standing orders.
“The LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest” — presence is a traveling mercy.
“Go, and do thou likewise” — mercy is commanded in the second person singular.

pos: v. (to utter, declare; rendering Hebrew amar, Greek lego)
etymology: Old English secgan. The Bible's third verse gives the verb its highest work: And God said. Everything else in Scripture unfolds from what God says.
biblical_def: To say is to utter in words — and in Scripture, saying is the engine of creation and revelation. “And God said, Let there be light: and there was light” (Gen 1:3): divine saying does not describe reality but produces it. At the bush God gives Moses His name as a saying to carry — “Thus shalt thou say unto the children of Israel, I AM hath sent me” (Exo 3:14) — and the Son speaks nothing on His own motion but what the Father gave Him to say (Joh 12:49). The redeemed inherit the verb: “Let the redeemed of the LORD say so” (Psa 107:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines say as to utter in words, to speak, to declare — common speech; Scripture's burden is whose saying stands.
webster_full: SAY, v.t. To utter in words; to speak; to declare; to pronounce.
2. To declare; to tell; to relate.
3. To affirm; to teach.
scriptures: Gen 1:3
And God said, Let there be light: and there was light.
Exo 3:14
And God said unto Moses, I AM THAT I AM: and he said, Thus shalt thou say unto the children of Israel, I AM hath sent me unto you.
Let the redeemed of the LORD say so, whom he hath redeemed from the hand of the enemy;
For I have not spoken of myself; but the Father which sent me, he gave me a commandment, what I should say, and what I should speak.
corruption_summary: Thus saith the LORD has been miniaturized into thus I feel and thus we affirm — pulpits that report the self's sayings while the divine saying that creates and commands goes unrepeated.
corruption_paragraphs: Preaching in Scripture is deputized saying: Moses carries a sentence he did not compose, and the prophets' formula — thus saith the LORD — claims nothing for the speaker and everything for the Sender. The corruption is not merely liberal denial of the formula but evangelical replacement of it, where the sermon's real authority is the anecdote and the congregation leaves knowing the preacher's heart rather than God's word. What God has said is the only saying with creative force.

The redeemed man's counter-discipline is confession in the old sense: saying back what God has said, and saying so aloud. “Let the redeemed of the LORD say so, whom he hath redeemed from the hand of the enemy” (Psa 107:2). Silence about redemption is not modesty; it is a broken echo. Faith comes by hearing, and hearing requires that somebody say.
roots_summary: Hebrew amar (H559), to say — the verb of Genesis 1's ten sayings; Greek lego (G3004), to say or declare, whose noun is logos, the Word.
roots_lines: Hebrew amar (H559) — to say; And God said, ten times over creation, and Thus saith the LORD through the prophets.
Greek lego (G3004) — to say, declare; Verily, verily, I say unto you — the Amen who speaks with original authority.
usage: “And God said, Let there be light” — divine saying produces what it pronounces.
“Thus shalt thou say… I AM hath sent me” — the preacher carries a sentence he did not compose.
“Let the redeemed of the LORD say so” — redemption obligates the tongue.

pos: v. (to form, fashion, cause to be; rendering Hebrew asah, Greek poieo)
etymology: Old English macian. Scripture opens with God making and closes with God making all things new; between the two, He makes fishers of men.
biblical_def: To make is to form and to cause to be. The counsel of the Godhead uses it at man's creation — “Let us make man in our image, after our likeness” (Gen 1:26) — and the psalmist plants it against every self-made illusion: “it is he that hath made us, and not we ourselves” (Psa 100:3). In the gospels the Maker walks the shore and keeps making: “Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men” (Mat 4:19). The last book gives the verb its final future: “Behold, I make all things new” (Rev 21:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines make as to form of materials, to fashion, to cause to exist — and Scripture reserves the deepest making, out of nothing and unto newness, for God alone.
webster_full: MAKE, v.t. To form of materials; to fashion; to mold into shape; to cause to exist.
2. To create; to cause to exist from nothing.
3. To compose; to constitute; to cause to be or become.
scriptures: Gen 1:26

And God said, Let us make man in our image, after our likeness: and let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the fowl of the air, and over the cattle, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creepeth upon the earth.
Know ye that the LORD he is God: it is he that hath made us, and not we ourselves; we are his people, and the sheep of his pasture.
Mat 4:19
And he saith unto them, Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men.
Rev 21:5
And he that sat upon the throne said, Behold, I make all things new. And he said unto me, Write: for these words are true and faithful.
corruption_summary: The self-made man is the age's founding myth — identity, truth, and even the body treated as raw material for self-manufacture — a direct inversion of it is he that hath made us.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 100 was written as a corrective the modern world has made newly necessary: know ye that the LORD he is God; it is he that hath made us, and not we ourselves. The entire architecture of self-invention — choose your truth, construct your identity, author your meaning — is a creature attempting the Creator's verb. What follows in the psalm is the sanity the myth forfeits: we are his people, and the sheep of his pasture. Madeness is not humiliation; it is belonging.

The gospel does not leave a man as it finds him, but neither does it hand him the tools of self-manufacture. I will make you, says Christ to fishermen — the remaking is His project, on His timetable, toward His design. If any man be in Christ, he is a new creature; and the voice from the throne that says Behold, I make all things new is the same voice that said Let there be light. Sanctification is being made, not making it.
roots_summary: Hebrew asah (H6213), to make or do, the workman verb of creation week; Greek poieo (G4160), to make or do, whose noun gives us the workmanship — poiema — of Ephesians 2:10.
roots_lines: Hebrew asah (H6213) — to make, do, accomplish; God made the firmament, the two great lights, and man from the dust.
Greek poieo (G4160) — to make, to do; I will make you fishers of men (Mat 4:19); we are his workmanship, poiema (Eph 2:10).
usage: “Let us make man in our image” — the counsel of the Godhead at the first making.
“It is he that hath made us, and not we ourselves” — the sentence the self-made myth cannot survive.
“Behold, I make all things new” — the last making, already begun in every new creature.

pos: v. (to set, place, lay; rendering Hebrew sum and nathan, Greek tithemi)
etymology: Late Old English putian. The plainest verb of placement, which Scripture uses for the deepest placements — man into Eden, sin away at the cross, the new man onto the believer.
biblical_def: To put is to set in place. God's putting begins in the garden — “the LORD God planted a garden eastward in Eden; and there he put the man whom he had formed” (Gen 2:8) — and reaches its summit at the cross, where Christ appeared “to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself” (Heb 9:26). The believer's daily obedience borrows the same verb: “put on the new man, which after God is created in righteousness” (Eph 4:24). And God puts gladness in the heart, more than in the time that corn and wine increased (Psa 4:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines put as to set, lay or place — the general word for placement; Scripture's question is always who places what, and where.
webster_full: PUT, v.t. To set, lay or place; in a general sense.
2. To place in any situation or condition.
3. To apply; to set to use or employment.
scriptures: Gen 2:8
And the LORD God planted a garden eastward in Eden; and there he put the man whom he had formed.
Heb 9:26
For then must he often have suffered since the foundation of the world: but now once in the end of the world hath he appeared to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself.
Eph 4:24
And that ye put on the new man, which after God is created in righteousness and true holiness.
Psa 4:7
Thou hast put gladness in my heart, more than in the time that their corn and their wine increased.
corruption_summary: A religion of self-placement — put yourself first, put it out into the universe — against a Bible in which the decisive puttings are all God's: man into the garden, sin out of the record, gladness into the heart.
corruption_paragraphs: Hebrews' phrase deserves more wonder than it gets: to put away sin. Not to manage, offset, or reframe it — to put it away, as a thing carried off the premises, by the sacrifice of Himself. Every religion of self-salvation is a man trying to relocate his own sin somewhere survivable; the gospel announces the relocation already accomplished: as far as the east is from the west, so far hath he removed our transgressions from us.

What is left for the believer is the wardrobe verb: put off the old man, put on the new. The order of Ephesians matters — the new man is created already, in righteousness and true holiness; putting him on is not self-manufacture but getting dressed in what grace has tailored. Mortification and vivification, the Puritans called the two motions; Paul called them putting off and putting on, and made them daily wear.
roots_summary: Hebrew sum (H7760), to set or place, and nathan (H5414), to give or set; Greek tithemi (G5087), to place — the shepherd putting down His life belongs to the same family of placement.
roots_lines: Hebrew sum (H7760) — to put, set, place; there he put the man (Gen 2:8); thou hast put gladness in my heart (Psa 4:7).
Greek tithemi (G5087) — to put, lay, place; the good shepherd layeth down — putteth — his life for the sheep (Joh 10:11).
Greek enduo (G1746) — to put on as a garment; put on the new man (Eph 4:24), put on the Lord Jesus Christ (Rom 13:14).
usage: “And there he put the man whom he had formed” — placement is providence from the first garden.
“To put away sin by the sacrifice of himself” — the decisive relocation of guilt.
“Put on the new man” — grace tailors; obedience dresses.

pos: v. (to pull toward, attract; rendering Hebrew mashak, Greek helkuo)
etymology: Old English dragan, to drag or pull. Scripture uses it for wells and swords, but supremely for the Father's pull on a soul and the Son's pull from the cross.
biblical_def: To draw is to pull toward. Our Lord states the sinner's condition and God's remedy in one sentence: “No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him” (Joh 6:44) — coming is commanded, and the coming ones are drawn. Lifted up, the Son becomes the magnet of the world: “And I, if I be lifted up from the earth, will draw all men unto me” (Joh 12:32). The believer's part is the answering motion: “Draw nigh to God, and he will draw nigh to you” (Jas 4:8); “let us draw near with a true heart” (Heb 10:22).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines draw as to pull along, to bring by compulsion or by attraction — and the theology of grace turns on which of those two pullings God's drawing is.
webster_full: DRAW, v.t. To pull along; to cause to move toward the person or thing that pulls.
2. To attract; to cause to move or tend toward.
3. To pull out, as a sword from its sheath; to unsheathe.
scriptures: Joh 6:44
No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him: and I will raise him up at the last day.
And I, if I be lifted up from the earth, will draw all men unto me.
Jas 4:8
Draw nigh to God, and he will draw nigh to you. Cleanse your hands, ye sinners; and purify your hearts, ye double minded.
Let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience, and our bodies washed with pure water.
corruption_summary: Two ditches: a drawing reduced to polite influence any sinner may shrug off, or a drawing so mechanical that the drawn arrive without ever willingly coming — Scripture's cords are stronger than the first and kinder than the second.
corruption_paragraphs: The drawing of John 6:44 is no mere wooing, for it infallibly lands its object: and I will raise him up at the last day. Every one drawn arrives, and arrives at resurrection. But neither is it a hauling of the unwilling — Jeremiah's parallel gives the manner: with lovingkindness have I drawn thee. God draws a soul the way dawn draws open a flower, by giving it the life that makes it want the light. The Reformed name for this is effectual calling, and its instrument is ordinarily the lifted-up Christ preached.

James' imperative — draw nigh to God — is not a contradiction of sovereign drawing but its fruit walking. The drawn draw near. A Christian who pleads inability while neglecting the means of nearness has borrowed the doctrine's vocabulary against its purpose; Hebrews puts the two in order: having boldness by the blood of Jesus, let us draw near.
roots_summary: Hebrew mashak (H4900), to draw or drag — with lovingkindness have I drawn thee (Jer 31:3); Greek helkuo (G1670), to draw — the Father's drawing, the Son's drawing, and Peter's drawn sword share the verb.
roots_lines: Hebrew mashak (H4900) — to draw, drag, prolong; drawn with cords of a man, with bands of love (Hos 11:4).
Greek helkuo (G1670) — to draw; Joh 6:44 and 12:32 of souls, Joh 18:10 of a sword, Joh 21:11 of a net full of fishes.
usage: “No man can come to me, except the Father… draw him” — inability answered by drawing, not by despair.
“I, if I be lifted up… will draw all men unto me” — the cross is the world's magnet.
“Draw nigh to God, and he will draw nigh to you” — the drawn draw near.

pos: v. (to move swiftly; rendering Hebrew ruts, Greek trecho)
etymology: Old English rinnan. Scripture's runners include messengers, prodigals' fathers, and every saint entered in the race set before us.
biblical_def: To run is to move at full stretch, and the New Testament makes it the church's athletic figure: “let us run with patience the race that is set before us, looking unto Jesus” (Heb 12:1–2). Paul disciplines the figure — “So run, that ye may obtain” (1Co 9:24) — a race is not a stroll. The prophet promises the running strength renewed: “they shall run, and not be weary” (Isa 40:31); the psalmist locates the track: “I will run the way of thy commandments, when thou shalt enlarge my heart” (Psa 119:32).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines run as to move swiftly, so that both feet leave the ground at once — haste with the whole body; Scripture's concern is the direction and the endurance.
webster_full: RUN, v.i. To move or pass swiftly; to hasten in motion.
2. To contend in a race.
3. To flow; to move in a current, as a liquid.
scriptures: Heb 12:1

Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us,
Know ye not that they which run in a race run all, but one receiveth the prize? So run, that ye may obtain.
But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint.
I will run the way of thy commandments, when thou shalt enlarge my heart.
corruption_summary: Hustle culture baptized — running as identity, burnout as devotion — while the biblical race runs with patience, on a set course, looking at a fixed point that is not the runner.
corruption_paragraphs: Hebrews' race has three features modern striving lacks: it is set before us (the course is assigned, not invented), it is run with patience (endurance, not sprint-and-collapse), and it is run looking unto Jesus (the eyes are off the runner). Religious hustle keeps the exertion and loses all three — self-chosen course, unsustainable pace, eyes on the metrics. That race has no finish line because it has no author and finisher.

Psalm 119:32 supplies the physiology of holy running: I will run the way of thy commandments, when thou shalt enlarge my heart. Obedience at speed is not willpower but cardiac capacity, and God is the one who enlarges. Isaiah's runners likewise wait upon the LORD before they run without weariness — the stillness is the fuel of the speed.
roots_summary: Hebrew ruts (H7323), to run — messengers, warriors, and the strong man of Psalm 19 rejoicing to run his race; Greek trecho (G5143), to run, Paul's favorite athletic verb.
roots_lines: Hebrew ruts (H7323) — to run; which rejoiceth as a strong man to run a race (Psa 19:5).
Greek trecho (G5143) — to run; 1 Corinthians 9:24, Hebrews 12:1, Galatians 5:7 — ye did run well; who did hinder you?
usage: “Let us run with patience the race that is set before us” — assigned course, enduring pace, fixed gaze.
“So run, that ye may obtain” — the race is real and the prize is worth training for.
“I will run the way of thy commandments, when thou shalt enlarge my heart” — God supplies the cardiac capacity.

pos: v. (to lay hold of, receive; rendering Hebrew laqach, Greek lambano)
etymology: Late Old English tacan, from Norse. Discipleship's hardest imperative and grace's freest offer share this one verb.
biblical_def: To take is to lay hold of. Christ fixes it at the center of following Him — “If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me” (Mat 16:24) — and at the center of His own authority over His life: “I lay down my life, that I might take it again” (Joh 10:17). Grace turns the verb toward the empty-handed: “whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely” (Rev 22:17). The psalmist shows the taking that worship is: “I will take the cup of salvation, and call upon the name of the LORD” (Psa 116:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines take as to receive or seize into possession, to lay hold of — one verb for both gift and grip, which is exactly Scripture's usage.
webster_full: TAKE, v.t. To receive or accept what is offered.
2. To lay hold of; to seize; to grasp.
3. To receive into the mind; to understand.
scriptures: Then said Jesus unto his disciples, If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me.
Therefore doth my Father love me, because I lay down my life, that I might take it again.
I will take the cup of salvation, and call upon the name of the LORD.
And the Spirit and the bride say, Come. And let him that heareth say, Come. And let him that is athirst come. And whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely.
corruption_summary: A cross reduced to inconvenience — my commute is my cross — and a taking reduced to consuming: the age takes everything except the cross and the cup.
corruption_paragraphs: Take up his cross meant one thing to a first-century hearer: a condemned man carrying the instrument of his own execution. The corruption is domestication — the cross as metaphor for life's ordinary frictions. But the verse's own economy resists it: deny himself precedes take up, and what is denied is not dessert but the self's claim to itself. Daily cross-bearing (Luke adds daily) is the standing execution of self-rule, resumed each morning.

The same age that will not take the cross also cannot simply take the gift. The water of life is offered freely — without money and without price — yet religious man keeps reaching for it with a wallet, negotiating terms, earning standing. The two takings stand or fall together: only the hand opened by grace to take freely is free enough to take up a cross.
roots_summary: Hebrew laqach (H3947), to take, receive — Enoch was not, for God took him; Greek lambano (G2983), to take or receive — as many as received him is this verb.
roots_lines: Hebrew laqach (H3947) — to take, fetch, receive; God took the man and put him in the garden; God took Enoch (Gen 5:24).
Greek lambano (G2983) — to take, receive; take up the cross (Mat 16:24), and as many as received him (Joh 1:12).
usage: “Let him deny himself, and take up his cross” — the standing execution of self-rule.
“I lay down my life, that I might take it again” — no man takes what the Son has authority to take.
“Let him take the water of life freely” — grace prices its cup at nothing.

pos: v. (to be bound in duty; rendering Greek dei and opheilo)
etymology: The old past tense of owe: what one ought is what one owes. The word carries the whole grammar of moral obligation in five letters.
biblical_def: Ought names moral debt. The apostles wield it against every rival claim — “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29) — and the risen Lord uses it of His own path: “Ought not Christ to have suffered these things, and to enter into his glory?” (Luk 24:26). It binds worship's details — “these ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other undone” (Mat 23:23) — and it bends the church toward the basin: “ye also ought to wash one another's feet” (Joh 13:14). Obligation, in Scripture, is owed love with its sleeves rolled up.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines ought as to be held or bound in duty or moral obligation, citing this very verse — these ought ye to have done.
webster_full: OUGHT, v. imperfect. To be held or bound in duty or moral obligation. Matt. 23.
2. To be necessary; to behoove.
scriptures: Act 5:29
Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
Ought not Christ to have suffered these things, and to enter into his glory?

Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye pay tithe of mint and anise and cummin, and have omitted the weightier matters of the law, judgment, mercy, and faith: these ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other undone.
If I then, your Lord and Master, have washed your feet; ye also ought to wash one another's feet.
corruption_summary: A culture allergic to ought — obligation rebranded as trauma, duty dissolved into authenticity — while Scripture grounds the sweetest realities, from Christ's cross to washed feet, in holy necessity.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern self recognizes no debts it did not choose, so ought survives only as oppression's vocabulary. But the Emmaus road hangs redemption itself on the word: ought not Christ to have suffered? — a necessity rooted in covenant and prophecy, which the Son embraced freely and called His meat. Where ought is abolished, love loses its spine; the New Testament's obligations are love's owed shape: owe no man any thing, but to love one another.

Acts 5:29 marks the word's political edge. When commands collide, obligation stacks: we ought to obey God rather than men — not instead of men, but rather, a ranked debt. The church that has forgotten how to say ought will discover, when the collision comes, that it has nothing to stand on but preference — and preference folds.
roots_summary: Greek dei (G1163), it is necessary — the must of Christ's sufferings; opheilo (G3784), to owe — the debt-word of washed feet and mutual love.
roots_lines: Greek dei (G1163) — it is necessary, one must; ought not Christ to have suffered (Luk 24:26); ye must be born again (Joh 3:7).
Greek opheilo (G3784) — to owe, be indebted; ye also ought to wash one another's feet (Joh 13:14); we ought to lay down our lives for the brethren (1Jn 3:16).
usage: “We ought to obey God rather than men” — obligations rank, and God outranks.
“Ought not Christ to have suffered these things?” — redemption ran on holy necessity.
“Ye also ought to wash one another's feet” — owed love with a towel on.

pos: v. (to stir, impel, be shaken; rendering Hebrew mot, Greek phero and kineo)
etymology: From Latin moveo through French. Scripture's usage runs two directions: what God moves stands accomplished; what cannot be moved stands secure.
biblical_def: To move is to stir or displace — and Scripture's deepest uses are both negative and glorious. The fixed saint: “I have set the LORD always before me: because he is at my right hand, I shall not be moved” (Psa 16:8). The fixed city: God is in her midst, “she shall not be moved” (Psa 46:5). The moved prophets: “holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost” (2Pe 1:21) — borne along as a ship before wind. And the God in whom “we live, and move, and have our being” (Act 17:28) is Himself the unmoved ground of every motion.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines move as to impel, to carry or draw from one place to another, to excite into action, to affect or touch — motion of body and of heart together.
webster_full: MOVE, v.t. To impel; to carry, convey or draw from one place to another; to cause to change place.
2. To excite into action; to affect; to agitate.
3. To touch; to awaken the feelings; to affect with compassion.
scriptures: Psa 16:8
I have set the LORD always before me: because he is at my right hand, I shall not be moved.
Psa 46:5
God is in the midst of her; she shall not be moved: God shall help her, and that right early.
For the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man: but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost.
For in him we live, and move, and have our being; as certain also of your own poets have said, For we are also his offspring.
corruption_summary: A spirituality that chases being moved — the feeling as the proof — and a fragility that is moved by everything: Scripture prizes the opposite pair, saints unmoved by circumstance and Scripture moved by the Spirit.
corruption_paragraphs: 2 Peter 1:21 is the Reformed doctrine of inspiration in one clause: prophecy came not by the will of man, but holy men spake as they were moved — carried, as Luke uses the same word for a ship driven before the storm — by the Holy Ghost. The men were fully men, the words fully theirs, and the freight fully God's. Every theory that reduces Scripture to religious genius has swapped the mover; every reader who trembles at the word has identified Him correctly.

Meanwhile the psalmist's immovability is not stoicism but geography: because he is at my right hand, I shall not be moved. The believer's stability is positional — God's nearness, not the believer's nerve. A generation moved by every headline and algorithm is not more sensitive but worse anchored; the kingdom we receive cannot be moved (Heb 12:28), and its citizens borrow its steadiness.
roots_summary: Hebrew mot (H4131), to totter or be shaken — almost always with a negative: not be moved; Greek phero (G5342), to bear or carry — the Spirit's moving of the prophets; kineo (G2795), to set in motion.
roots_lines: Hebrew mot (H4131) — to totter, shake, slip; I shall not be moved (Psa 16:8); she shall not be moved (Psa 46:5).
Greek phero (G5342) — to bear, carry, drive; moved by the Holy Ghost (2Pe 1:21), the same verb as a ship driven before the wind (Act 27:15).
Greek kineo (G2795) — to move, stir; in him we live, and move, and have our being (Act 17:28).
usage: “Because he is at my right hand, I shall not be moved” — stability is positional, not temperamental.
“Holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost” — carried like a ship before wind: inspiration.
“In him we live, and move, and have our being” — every motion borrows from the Unmoved.
